newsitem.title: USA: Oil companies downplay global warming, author says.
newsitem.headline: Oil companies downplay global warming, author says.

text.p: The multi-billion dollar fossil fuel industry is promoting the work of dissenting scientists who question the existence or danger of global warming, according to a book published on Friday by an award-winning journalist.

The oil, gas and coal industries, which support the economies of many Middle East nations and have sales exceeding $2 billion a day, have used their wealth to create "a relentless drumbeat of doubt in the public's mind," about the veracity of global warming, author Ross Gelbspan said.

The fossil fuel lobby has spent millions of dollars to inflate the prominence of a small group of "greenhouse sceptics" in order to delay political action that might harm the industry, Gelbspan claims in his book "The Heat Is On."
"They have been able to create a general perception that the issue is hopelessly stuck in uncertainty," Gelbspan told insurance industry executives at a recent conference in Miami.

Gelbspan, who won a 1984 Pulitzer prize for a series in the Boston Globe on employment discrimination, said oil and coal companies mounted a costly campaign to persuade the public that fears of global warming were unwarranted.
They also wanted to create a perception that more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere could lead to increased growing seasons, better crop yields and reforestation.

"By keeping the discussion focused on whether there really is a problem, these dozen or so dissidents -- contradicting the consensus view held by 2,500 of the world's top climate scientists -- have until now prevented discussion about how to address the problem," he wrote.
Respected scientists have said global warming caused by an overload of carbon dioxide in the Earth's atmosphere could cause dramatic, worldwide climate changes.

Gelbspan argues that greenhouse effects are already being felt in unprecedented natural events including floods, more frequent and intense hurricanes and infestations of disease-carrying insects. He cited as examples recent flooding in the Pacific Northwest and Chicago's 1995 killer heat wave.
Continued warming, he argues, could result in outbreaks of disease caused by increased insect populations and billions of dollars in insured losses from rising sea levels.
Yet oil and gas companies have mounted a disinformation campaign to delay a move away from carbon-based energy as a way of preserving their corporate bottom line, he said.
Gelbspan cited a video produced by Western Fuels Association Inc, a coal industry group.
"The video's aim is to persuade policymakers that a warmer, wetter, carbon dioxide-enhanced world would be, contrary to the alarms of environmentalists, a godsend," Gelbspan wrote.

Arizona State University professor Dr. Robert Balling, one of the "dissenting" scientists named by Gelbspan, conceded that part of his university's research funding came from the fossil fuel industry and said energy companies "absolutely" promoted science favourable to their views, as do environmental groups.
"As far as promoting a viewpoint, they are free to do whatever they want," Balling said.

"I believe that it is true that humans are having some impact on climate. Humans have altered atmospheric chemistry," he said. But "if we're having some effect, the overall effect would be extremely small."

Fredrick Palmer, general manager of Western Fuels, told the insurance executives that the lifestyle of U.S. consumers was threatened by a pessimistic coalition of bureaucrats and environmentalists who have made "arbritrary assumptions ... to forecast an apocalypse a hundred years from now."

Palmer, who calls coal "clean" energy, said the notion that carbon dioxide was a pollutant threatened the economies of industrial nations and millions of U.S. jobs would be lost to developing nations if the United States "decarbonizes."
"Instead of vilifying coal, we have to get on our knees and thank the Lord that we have it in such abundance," he said.
